`_cache/shiller_sp500.parquet` (never re-fetched live). As-of **2026-06-14**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n months | Fingerprint (cpi_yoy) |
|---|---|--:|---|
| Shiller S&P 500 monthly | 1872-01 to 2023-06 | 1,818 | `b2019f787713` |

Inflation regime split: CPI YoY > 3% = **high** (724 months); <= 3% = **low** (1,094 months).
Threshold is pre-specified at 3%; the 1970s-1980s episodes account for most of the high-
inflation cluster.

## The Fisher Hypothesis for Stocks

A perfect inflation hedge requires nominal equity returns to rise **one-for-one** with
inflation (Fisher beta = 1.0), leaving *real* returns invariant.

| Regression | OLS beta | HAC t-stat | R² | Interpretation |
|---|--:|--:|--:|---|
| Nominal 12m return ~ CPI YoY | **+0.31** | **+1.30** | 0.010 | Only 31c per 1pp of CPI — far below 1.0 |
| Real TR 12m return ~ CPI YoY | **-0.72** | **-3.02** | 0.044 | Real returns *fall* when inflation rises |

The nominal Fisher beta of **+0.31** is far below the full-hedge value of 1.0, and its HAC
t-stat of **+1.30** does not clear the inference bar (|t| < 2). Stocks absorb only a third
of each percentage point of inflation in their nominal returns. The remainder hits real
purchasing power: the real-return Fisher beta of **-0.72** is significant (HAC t = **-3.02**)
and negative — the opposite of hedging. This replicates the core Fama & Schwert (1977)
finding across the full 150-year Shiller panel.

## Regime Analysis — Does High-Inflation Predict Lower Forward Real Returns?

Pre-specified 3% CPI YoY split; forward returns from month *t* onward (no look-ahead).
The **shuffled-label control** permutes the regime label to show what a false-positive
regime difference looks like (expected near-zero t-stat).

### Forward 1-Year Real Total Return

| Regime | n months | Mean pa | Std |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| High inflation (CPI > 3%) | 713 | **+4.3%** | 19.5% |
| Low inflation (CPI ≤ 3%) | 1,093 | **+11.4%** | 19.0% |
| **Difference (high − low)** | — | **−7.1 pp** | — |
| HAC t-stat (difference) | — | **−4.08** | — |
| Shuffled-label control t | — | +0.79 | — |

The 7 percentage point gap in 1-year forward real returns is **statistically real** (|t| = 4.08 >>
2). The shuffled-label control produces t = 0.79, confirming the real gap is not a random
split artefact. Stocks earned half the real return in high-inflation regimes as in
low-inflation ones.

### Forward 5-Year Annualised Real Total Return

| Regime | n months | Mean pa | Std |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| High inflation (CPI > 3%) | ~700 | **+6.0%** | 8.1% |
| Low inflation (CPI ≤ 3%) | ~1,058 | **+7.9%** | 7.4% |
| **Difference (high − low)** | — | **−1.9 pp** | — |
| HAC t-stat (difference) | — | **−2.11** | — |

Over 5-year horizons the regime gap narrows substantially (from 7pp to 2pp), consistent with
stocks functioning as a *long-run* real asset even if not a *short-run* hedge. The gap is
still statistically real at the 5-year horizon (|t| = 2.11).

## The Honest Verdict

The famous Fama & Schwert (1977) / Modigliani & Cohn (1979) finding replicates cleanly:

- **The short-run inflation hedge is a myth.** Nominal returns absorb only ~31% of inflation;
  real returns fall by ~0.72pp per pp of CPI inflation, with a HAC t-stat of -3.02.
- **High-inflation regimes are genuinely bad for equities in real terms** — a 7pp forward
  1-year gap (HAC t = -4.08), robust to shuffled-label control.
- **Over 5 years, stocks partially recover** their role as a real asset (-1.9pp gap,
  HAC t = -2.11) — consistent with the long-run view, but the short-run damage is real.

### Signal: MIXED

The *negative* inflation-hedge effect (real returns fall when inflation rises) is statistically
real and significant on both 1-year (t = -4.08) and 5-year (t = -2.11) horizons. The positive
claim (stocks *are* a hedge) is false at short horizons and only partially true at long ones.
The verdict is MIXED: the effect is real, but it is the *opposite* of what the folk wisdom
asserts.

### Tradability: MIRAGE

Inflation regimes are broad macro epochs (the 1970s, the post-GFC era), not actionable timing
signals. You cannot systematically rotate out of equities based on a CPI print and back in at
the right time. The regime effect is real for description and risk awareness; it is not a
timing edge. MIRAGE.
